articles.title: AI selloff pushes S&P 500 and Dow into correction as Nasdaq erases its 2026 gains
articles.subtitle: The Nasdaq’s worst week since March 2020 hit chip stocks hardest, and futures rebounded Monday as traders reassessed Federal Reserve rate bets
articles.excerpt: An AI-led selloff on Friday pushed the S&P 500 and the Dow into correction territory and erased the Nasdaq’s gains for 2026, with the S&P 500 down 3.7% for a seventh straight loss, before U.S. stock futures rebounded sharply on Monday.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: How deep the week’s losses ran
Why chip stocks led the drop
Bonds and the Fed’s rate path
What it means for mortgage rates

content.text: U.S. stocks sank on Friday in a selloff led by chipmakers and other AI-linked companies, pushing the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average into correction territory and wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39, its seventh straight daily loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020, according to Fox Business and closing data carried by Yahoo Finance.
The Dow lost 949.77 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73, which Fox Business described as its second-largest single-day point drop on record.

Stock futures bounced early Monday. Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 3.3%, S&P 500 futures about 2.5% and Dow futures about 1.9% ahead of the U.S. open, according to Reuters figures relayed by Beinsure. Pre-market moves can fade or reverse once regular trading begins, and the cash session had not opened when this article was written.
How deep the week’s losses ran

The S&P 500 and the Dow each closed more than 10% below their record highs, the usual threshold for a correction. Weekly summaries of Friday’s closing data put the S&P 500’s decline for the week at about 8.6%, the Nasdaq Composite’s at about 10% and the Dow’s at about 8%. Fox Business reported that the S&P 500 had its worst week since April 2025, while Bloomberg reported that the Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since March 2020 after falling 5.6% on Friday alone.

Volatility spiked. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, closed at 35.89, up about 26% on the day, and Bloomberg said it was at its highest level since April 2025. The selling was global: the MSCI World Index fell 3.4%.

It was the second major AI-linked rout this month. On Nov. 5, the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, its worst day since April 2025, as worries that data-center construction will slow because of higher borrowing costs weighed on AI stocks, the Associated Press reported.
Why chip stocks led the drop

Semiconductor shares took the worst of it. A closely watched chip gauge sank 11%, Bloomberg reported. Nvidia fell 14.01% to close at $125.53, while Advanced Micro Devices dropped about 13.3% to $424.32 and Broadcom about 12.1% to $304.65, according to The Motley Fool. Micron fell nearly 14%, according to Dim Sum Daily.

Nvidia’s slide followed a Reuters report that Securities and Exchange Commission staff are examining possible accounting issues at the company, according to Bloomberg and other outlets. Neither Nvidia nor the SEC had confirmed an inquiry in the coverage reviewed for this article, and an investigation by itself does not establish wrongdoing. The stock fell even though Nvidia had reported strong quarterly results and raised its outlook earlier in the week, The Motley Fool reported.

Analysts pointed to a broader reassessment of AI spending. Richard Saperstein of Treasury Partners cited a repricing of AI expectations, slower data-center expansion, tighter funding for AI projects and moderating tech earnings growth, according to Dim Sum Daily. Anthropic, which began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after pricing its IPO at $83 a share, fell 8.5% to $88.91 in its second session, giving back part of a 17% first-day gain, according to Fox Business.
Bonds and the Fed’s rate path

Investors rushed into government bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.9% on Friday from 5.04% a day earlier, according to Bloomberg and Yahoo Finance data. On Monday it rose about 5 basis points to 4.96% as that flight to safety eased, Reuters reported.

The moves reshaped bets on the Federal Reserve. The central bank raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on Sept. 16 and held on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, according to a meeting preview from Admirals. Governor Christopher Waller said on CNBC on Nov. 18 that if the Fed does not clearly signal a January move, “you have to go 50 in December,” Admirals reported, and CME FedWatch readings earlier in the week put the odds of a quarter-point December increase at 90% to 97%. October core consumer prices had risen 0.3%, above the 0.2% forecast.

After Friday’s selloff, Bloomberg reported that traders no longer fully priced in a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8–9 meeting, and CME FedWatch data cited by CoinDesk showed the probability of a half-point hike falling to zero from about 10%. Neil Dutta of Renaissance Macro Research cautioned that a Fed pullback could reignite inflation, Bloomberg reported.
What it means for mortgage rates

Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury yield. Freddie Mac’s latest weekly survey, released Nov. 19 before Friday’s bond rally, showed the average 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.28% from 7.11%, which ended four straight weekly declines; a year earlier it was 6.26%. The 15-year fixed rate averaged 6.66%, up from 6.45% a week earlier and 5.54% a year ago, WRE News reported from the release.

By News Editors’ calculation, principal and interest on a $400,000, 30-year loan would be about $2,737 a month at 7.28%, roughly $46 more than at 7.11%, before taxes, insurance and closing costs. Freddie Mac notes that its figures are national survey averages, not individual loan quotes. Whether Friday’s drop in yields reaches borrowers depends on whether it lasts; the next weekly survey should begin to show, and Monday’s partial rebound in yields is a reminder of how quickly the picture can change.
What to watch this week

Monday’s futures gains followed steps by Asian regulators to support markets: Taiwan tightened short-selling rules and Chinese exchanges eased margin-financing conditions, Reuters reported. In pre-market trading, Nvidia rose about 8% and Anthropic about 3%, after falling 14% and 8.5% on Friday, respectively.

Analysts were divided on what comes next. Chris Larkin of E*Trade from Morgan Stanley noted that only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 became bear markets, Bloomberg reported. Jonathan Krinsky of BTIG said that trading below the 200-day moving average “shifts risks to the downside,” and Massimo Santicchia of Procyon described sentiment as “decisively risk-off,” according to Dim Sum Daily. All three major averages slipped below their 200-day moving averages on Friday.

The calendar is crowded. The Fed’s October PCE inflation report is due Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Admirals; U.S. markets are closed Thursday, Nov. 26, for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday, Nov. 27, according to Swingfolio; and the Fed’s next policy meeting runs Dec. 8–9, according to the Federal Reserve’s calendar. Because market figures change quickly and some of those above are pre-market, readers should check live quotes. This article is general information, not investment advice.

articles.title: Gold hits three-month high as Treasury boosts bond buyback program
articles.subtitle: A weaker dollar and geopolitical tension are adding to the rally
articles.excerpt: Gold climbed to its highest level in roughly three months after the Treasury Department unexpectedly expanded its long-term bond buyback program, extending a rally fueled by a softer dollar, persistent inflation and Middle East tensions, though the metal remains well off the record highs it set earlier in the year.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: A rockier year than it looks

content.text: Gold prices climbed to their highest level in roughly three months this week, extending a rally that gained fresh momentum after the U.S. Treasury Department unexpectedly moved to expand its long-term bond buyback program.
Why gold is rallying

Analysts point to a combination of factors behind the move: continued tension in the Middle East, a softer U.S. dollar, and inflation that has stayed well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for years. The Treasury's decision to significantly increase the size of its long-term bond buybacks per session added fresh momentum, with the move interpreted by some traders as an effort to support liquidity in a bond market that has grown increasingly volatile, including a 30-year Treasury yield that briefly topped 5.2%, its highest level since 2007, after the Fed's contentious July rate decision.
A rockier year than it looks

The rally follows a rougher stretch for the precious metal earlier in the year: after touching record highs in January, gold suffered its worst quarterly decline in more than a decade before spending much of the summer largely range-bound. This month's renewed climb has lifted prices back toward, though still below, those January peaks, underscoring how choppy the metal's path has been even as its overall direction this year has trended higher.
What investors are watching next

Traders are closely watching upcoming inflation data along with remarks from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who has resisted giving markets forward guidance on the central bank's next move since taking over the role earlier this year. Three regional Fed presidents dissented at the July meeting in favor of raising rates, the first time in nearly a decade that three policymakers have dissented in the same hawkish direction, and minutes from that meeting showed several officials warning that financial conditions may not yet be tight enough to bring inflation back to target. Higher-for-longer interest rates and a still-elevated dollar have historically weighed on gold, making the metal's ability to hold its recent gains a closely watched signal for the broader market heading into the fall.

articles.title: Fed holds rates steady in 9-3 vote as three regional presidents dissent in favor of a hike
articles.subtitle: Three regional presidents dissented in favor of a rate increase
articles.excerpt: The Federal Reserve voted 9-3 to hold interest rates steady in July, with three regional bank presidents dissenting in favor of raising rates, the first time in nearly a decade that three policymakers have dissented in the same direction, sending the 30-year Treasury yield to its highest level since 2007.
articles.author: admin

content.text: The Federal Reserve voted 9-3 to hold its benchmark interest rate steady at its July meeting, in a decision publicly marked by an unusually sharp internal disagreement, as three regional Federal Reserve Bank presidents dissented in favor of raising rates immediately.
A rare hawkish split

The Federal Open Market Committee kept the federal funds rate in a target range of 3.5% to 3.75%, extending a hold that has now lasted five consecutive meetings following three rate cuts in late 2025. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan all dissented, each preferring a quarter-point increase; it was the first time since September 2016 that three policymakers dissented with a unified view of which direction rates should move, and analysts described the committee as containing a newly vocal bloc of hawks. No members of the Fed's Board of Governors joined the dissent.
The chairman's approach

The split presented an early test for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who has pushed back against giving markets detailed forward guidance on the central bank's next move, arguing the committee needs to observe how markets react to developments "direct and unfiltered" rather than pre-committing to a path. "I want to stress, of course, that decisions by this committee matter a great deal, and where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act," Warsh told reporters after the meeting. President Trump, who has pushed for lower rates, said afterward that Warsh was "a brilliant guy" who would personally prefer lower rates but was constrained by what the president called a "political" board.
How markets reacted

Markets reacted sharply. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed roughly 1,100 points lower on the day, its worst single-day performance in more than a year, while Treasury yields spiked: the 30-year Treasury yield jumped past 5.2%, its highest level since 2007, and the 10-year yield rose more than seven basis points to 4.677%. Mortgage rates, which tend to track longer-term Treasury yields, also drifted higher in the days that followed.
What the minutes later revealed

Minutes from the meeting, released three weeks later, showed the hawkish sentiment extended well beyond the three formal dissenters. The minutes quoted participants saying that "policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline," with some officials adding that current financial conditions might not yet be restrictive enough to bring inflation back to the Fed's 2% target. Separately, Bloomberg reported that two non-voting regional presidents, Kansas City's Jeffrey Schmid and St. Louis's Alberto Musalem, indicated they too would have backed a rate increase had they held a vote in July. Since the meeting, incoming data has complicated the picture: nonfarm payrolls fell in July and core inflation readings came in softer than feared, pulling back market expectations for a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September.

articles.title: Mortgage rates hold in the mid-6% range as bond market stays volatile
articles.subtitle: Freddie Mac forecasts rates will stay elevated through the rest of 2026
articles.excerpt: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has held around 6.6% this month even as bond market volatility keeps a clear direction hard to pin down, with Freddie Mac now forecasting rates will climb toward 6.8% by year-end as elevated Treasury yields offset softer housing data.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: A brief dip from a Treasury move
The outlook for the rest of 2026

content.text: Mortgage rates have held in the mid-6% range through much of August, with the average 30-year fixed rate ticking down slightly to around 6.6% even as broader bond market volatility keeps a clear direction for rates hard to pin down.
A brief dip from a Treasury move

The dip came after the Treasury Department said it would increase its buyback of long-term bonds in an effort to stabilize the bond market and boost liquidity, a move that briefly pushed 10-year Treasury note yields lower. Mortgage rates, which tend to track those yields closely, eased in response, though the effect proved short-lived against the backdrop of a bond market still absorbing the fallout from the Federal Reserve's contentious July meeting, when the 30-year Treasury yield briefly topped 5.2%, its highest level since 2007, after three regional Fed presidents dissented in favor of a rate hike.
Competing pressures on rates

Housing economists describe the current environment as a tug of war between softer housing data, which would typically pull rates lower, and elevated long-term Treasury yields driven by concerns over government deficits, inflation and broader economic uncertainty. Ongoing tension in the Middle East has also continued to affect energy prices, adding another layer of volatility to the bond market even as diplomatic progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz has periodically eased those pressures.
The outlook for the rest of 2026

Government-backed mortgage buyer Freddie Mac has revised its forecast higher, now projecting that the 30-year fixed rate will reach roughly 6.8% by the end of the year and remain in a similar range through 2027, a notable jump from its outlook just a month earlier. Purchase mortgage volume has slowed as a result, even as housing inventory has grown slightly and affordability has improved modestly compared with a year ago. Separately, New York Fed data released this month showed mortgage balances actually declined by $74 billion in the second quarter to $13.1 trillion, even as other categories of household debt, including auto loans and credit cards, continued to climb, a divergence economists attribute in part to elevated rates keeping would-be sellers locked into older, cheaper mortgages rather than listing their homes.

articles.title: Credit card debt approaches record as delinquency data draws new scrutiny
articles.subtitle: The New York Fed says much of the rise reflects old debts, not new financial stress
articles.excerpt: U.S. credit card balances climbed to $1.26 trillion in the second quarter, nearing last year's record, even as total household debt edged down slightly, according to the New York Fed, which says the pattern reflects a 'K-shaped economy' in which roughly 60% of the 175 million Americans with cards carry ongoing balances.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Total U.S. household debt edged down slightly in the second quarter, but credit card balances climbed to $1.26 trillion, nearing an all-time high, according to the latest quarterly household debt report from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
The headline numbers

The report, based on a nationally representative sample of anonymized credit data, found that total household debt fell $13 billion, or about 0.1%, to $18.8 trillion. Mortgage balances led the decline, dropping $74 billion to $13.1 trillion, while auto loan balances rose $28 billion to a record $1.71 trillion and home equity lines of credit climbed $13 billion to $459 billion. Credit card balances rose $21 billion, a 1.7% quarterly increase, to $1.26 trillion, edging closer to the $1.28 trillion record set in the fourth quarter of last year. Student loan balances, meanwhile, fell $7 billion to $1.65 trillion. "Delinquency rates across most products have held steady over the past two years," said Joelle Scally, economic policy advisor at the New York Fed. "Still, new delinquencies for auto loans and credit cards remain at elevated levels, a trend we'll continue to monitor."
A 'K-shaped economy'

Roughly 175 million Americans hold credit cards, and New York Fed researchers said about 60% of them do not pay off their balances in full each month, leaving those households carrying ongoing interest-bearing debt. "To us it reflects this K-shaped economy," researchers said on a press call accompanying the report, pointing to a growing divide between households with a financial cushion and those living paycheck to paycheck, vulnerable to a single unexpected expense tipping them into delinquency.
A more complicated delinquency picture

A separate, widely circulated statistic has fueled concern that American households are falling behind on credit card payments at a pace not seen since the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis: the share of credit card balances in "late-stage delinquency," or more than 90 days past due, jumped from 7.6% to 12.8% between the third quarter of 2022 and the first quarter of 2026. New York Fed researchers pushed back on that headline reading in a companion blog post, cautioning that the figure is a lagging indicator that largely reflects a growing pool of older, already charged-off debts that have continued to sit on credit reports for longer than they once did, rather than a fresh wave of borrowers newly falling behind. In earlier years, the researchers said, banks tended to remove those stale, charged-off debts from credit reports sooner, which had kept the older delinquency measure looking artificially low by comparison. New credit card delinquency transitions, the more forward-looking measure the researchers say is the better signal to watch, have stayed elevated but essentially flat over the past year, with 6.97% of balances transitioning into some stage of delinquency.

articles.title: Dow closes above 54,000 for the first time as earnings season impresses
articles.subtitle: The S&P 500 also notched a fresh record on hopes for progress in the Middle East
articles.excerpt: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 54,000 for the first time and the S&P 500 notched its first record close in two months, powered by a 29.5% surge in Palantir shares and a strong Caterpillar earnings beat, as falling oil prices reflected optimism over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Palantir and Caterpillar lead the way

content.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 54,000 points for the first time on August 4, while the S&P 500 notched its first record closing high in two months, as strong corporate earnings and easing tensions around a key Middle East shipping route lifted investor sentiment.
A record powered by earnings

The Dow jumped 907.47 points, or 1.71%, to close at 54,085.88, notching back-to-back record highs after clinching its first all-time high in a month the previous session. The S&P 500 gained 136.02 points, or 1.79%, to finish at a record 7,736.52, surpassing its previous closing peak from early June, while the Nasdaq Composite surged 671.10 points, or 2.59%, to 26,584.99, though it remained about 2% below its own record set earlier in the summer.
Palantir and Caterpillar lead the way

Palantir Technologies soared 29.5%, its second-best trading day on record, after chief executive Alex Karp said quarterly revenue jumped 93% to $1.94 billion in what he called an "otherworldly" quarter, with U.S. commercial revenue up 149% and the company raising its full-year revenue guidance by roughly $498 million to about $8.15 billion. Caterpillar, widely watched as a bellwether for the global industrial economy, climbed 5.6% after raising its own annual revenue growth forecast, with executives crediting demand for its power-generation and construction equipment tied to the ongoing buildout of AI data centers; the move made Caterpillar the single biggest contributor to the Dow's advance, adding roughly 280 points to the index.
A strong earnings season overall

The gains came in the middle of a robust second-quarter earnings season: of the 304 S&P 500 companies that had reported results by the prior Friday, 85.2% had beaten analyst estimates, well above the long-term average of 67.5%. Oil prices fell more than 5% on the day on growing conviction that a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping was close, while Treasury yields pulled back after spiking the previous week. Investors were also parsing SpaceX's first-ever earnings report as a newly public company, with shares of the rocket maker rising 9% to $125, still below its IPO target price of $135. Markets traded in a narrower band in the sessions that followed, with major indexes moving modestly as investors weighed inflation data and looked ahead to Nvidia's closely watched earnings report later in the month.

articles.title: Nasdaq gains as chip stocks rally ahead of Nvidia earnings
articles.subtitle: Investors positioned cautiously as bond yields eased for a second session
articles.excerpt: The Nasdaq Composite led U.S. markets higher as semiconductor stocks rallied and Treasury yields fell for a second straight session, with investors positioning ahead of Nvidia's closely watched earnings report and weighing a weaker consumer confidence reading and a worsening U.S.-Canada trade dispute.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Trade tensions add to the mix

content.text: U.S. stocks rose modestly on August 24, with the Nasdaq Composite leading the major indexes higher as a rally in semiconductor stocks helped offset broader caution ahead of Nvidia's closely watched earnings report later in the week.
Treasury yields ease again

Treasury yields fell for a second consecutive session, with the benchmark 10-year yield dropping more than seven basis points, providing additional support to equities. The move followed reports that the Treasury Department could tap its General Account to help fund bond repurchases, a development traders said eased some lingering concerns about bond market liquidity after yields had spiked sharply following the Federal Reserve's contentious July rate decision, when the 30-year Treasury yield briefly topped 5.2%, its highest level since 2007.
Trade tensions add to the mix

Sentiment was tempered somewhat by a weaker-than-expected consumer confidence reading and signs of a worsening trade dispute between the United States and Canada, which weighed on some segments of the market even as the broader indexes advanced. Oil prices fell more than 3% during the session, adding to a broader pullback in energy markets that has coincided with diplomatic progress on reopening key Middle East shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran and Oman were separately discussing a temporary joint shipping corridor around the same time.

Investors were largely positioning ahead of Nvidia's results, due after markets closed on August 26 and widely seen as a bellwether for the health of AI-related capital spending heading into the rest of the year. Nvidia went on to report fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and guided to $108 billion for the current quarter, results that came in well above the consensus estimates analysts had penciled in ahead of the report.
